searchText: As per the discussion in the ACD meeting today, proposing a breakout room meeting. Topic: EIP-2718 discussion contd. Date & Time: Nov 16, 2020 at 1500 UTC Duration: 60 mins I will send out a calendar invite tomorrow at 1400 UTC if there is no disagreement in date and time. Main topic of discussion I think is the Transaction format specifics for 2930 and 2972. Okay! I'll update the topic and create an agenda. Topic is OK, just wanted to use that statement as a jumping off point. 🙂 https://github.com/ethereum/pm/issues/223 Thanks <@!642887713246150666> ! 2972 as currently written: ```js // transaction - using SSZ-compatible format so we don't have to decode-extract-encode in order to validate signature 0x00 || yParity || r || s || 0x65000000 || rlp(nonce, gasPrice, gasLimit, to, value, data) // which is identical to 0x00 || ssz([yParity, r, s, rlp(nonce, gasPrice, gasLimit, to, value, data)]) // which is identical to ssz([0x00, yParity, r, s, rlp(nonce, gasPrice, gasLimit, to, value, data)]) // receipt - SSZ encoded 0 || status || cumulativeGasUsed || logsBloom || 0x09010000 || ssz(logs) // which is identical to 0 || ssz([status, cumulativeGasUsed, logsBloom, logs]) // which is identical to ssz([0, status, cumulativeGasUsed, logsBloom, logs]) ``` Per feedback on 2930, I suspect there will be pushback on this (as <@!543900561460822016> implied in the call). The minimal change from legacy encoding would look like this: ```js // transaction - mostly rlp encoded 0x00 || rlp([nonce, gasPrice, gasLimit, to, value, data, v, r, s]) // receipt - mostly rlp encoded 0x00 || rlp([status, cumulativeGasUsed, logsBloom, logs]) ``` In the minimal-change case, we are still bit packing stuff into `v` here (not separating out `chainId`) and verification is "annoying" in that you have to decode, parse, encode, validate. You also cannot validate without speaking RLP (unlike SSZ, where you can validate without SSZ due to the fact that SSZ is basically a fixed offset encoding for the most part). Unfortunately, for the receipt we can't do "SSZ-like", we have to *actually* use SSZ. Couldn't make the call this morning. I'll listen to the recording. However it's there a concise summary of what the push back is on 2718 No pushback on 2718 really. Just a general agreement that we should include 2972 in Berlin. But that means we have to decide on the format of transactions in 2972 ASAP. 🙂 To SSZ or not to SSZ. If advocate for us to not assume people will push back on ssz unless someone actually is There has been some light pushback on SSZ mainly because it is a change, and change is risky, especially when we are in a hurry to get Berlin out. Does anyone know offhand what the variable length data pointer formatting is in SSZ? Is it number of bytes from start of fixed portion, or number of bytes from end of fixed portion, and is it prefixed with a sentinel byte? Ah, right. Little endian format as well. (answer is: the offset is in bytes from beginning of payload) Is `cumulativeGasUsed` a `uint256`? Seems a bit ridiculous to have it be as such. That extra padding for SSZ in the legacy wrapped transaction I guess is negligible, and could go through. But what if any subsequent format would become rather complex to maintain SSZ compatibility and therefore it is decided not to be SSZ compatible. What happens in that case? I like having SSZ compatibility, but it would be really good to have some general buy-in and not a sneaky approach. What kind of thing would ssz not be able to support? > I like having SSZ compatibility, but it would be really good to have some general buy-in and not a sneaky approach. <@!425279588009246720> I agree. I *think* there is general buy in on SSZ eventually, and my (weak) argument is "why not now". It is not about SSZ not being able to support something, albeit people can argue whether it can efficiently encode everything needed. It is rather about the fact that the transaction format is **not** ssz encoded in the eyes of the client. It just happens to be compatible. The counterargument to "why not now" is because "we are in a hurry now and it isn't critical now". I don't think SSZ vs rlp makes this go any faster Each transaction type can use its own encoding, so deciding on RLP for 2930 and 2972 wouldn't prevent us from using SSZ in 1559 or 2711. I think that is even less ideal to have both RLP and SSZ encoded new transactions. I could see a lot of pushback to adding SSZ versions once RLP versions are already out. I think ETH1.x will *eventually* have to include SSZ libraries? Is this correct? That is, ETH1 and ETH2 cannot merge until ETH1 clients have SSZ support? I don't think there's such a strict requirement. It depends on the not-yet-decided method how eth1 gets data from eth2. That does strengthen the "stick with RLP" argument then. I personally would be totally in favour of getting rid of RLP! Though, it is a tad frustrating because it does seem like most people agree that RLP is not a good fit for transaction/receipt encoding. Nobody likes rlp... Who's actually pushing back and saying "no" And there are supposedly some cool things we can do with proofs if we move to SSZ (that I don't understand). But that is a personal preference only. And I think the only way to get it achieved if there is some buy-in and not through the backdoors. <@!364458974906548225> there was some pushback a couple of ACDs ago when the discussion shifted to the transaction receipts / blocks. Where one would need to consider introducing some sort of new encoding as well for hashing. I don't see this as a backdoor. Nobody is sneaking this in. I think introducing SSZ will significantly delay 2718+2930 That is under the assumption that adding SSZ support isn't as simple as including some package that was already developed and tested by the ETH2 team? I don't know what languages already have SSZ support (for various reasons), or whether that support is in a nice easy-to-consume package. The geth team would need to weigh in, but I would expect them to want to develop it themselves Implementing full SSZ support vs the support needed to decode a known transaction format with a known schema should be less than a day of work. https://github.com/ethereum/eth2.0-specs/blob/dev/ssz/simple-serialize.md#implementations > Implementing full SSZ support vs the support needed to decode a known transaction format with a known schema should be less than a day of work. <@!364458974906548225> Unfortunately, I think that may not be true for receipts. 😢 right, they have more complexity In particular, receipts have `logs` as the last item, and each log is variable width itself I believe. And it seems weird to have a transaction SSZ encoded and its receipt RLP encoded. But maybe that is an acceptable compromise to people? even still, SSZ isn't that complex I think we should stop assuming there is pushback and actually find out You should come to the breakout meeting <@!364458974906548225>, you can champion SSZ! (so I don't have to) i prefer to not support SSZ <https://discordapp.com/channels/595666850260713488/751450632543535236/776833293495959555> > Date & Time: Nov 16, 2020 at 1500 UTC <@!364458974906548225> ☝️ Found it, yeah, I can do that. Is there a calendar invite? Calendar invite going out tomorrow. I don't know how to get on the list. Probably just tell <@!642887713246150666>. <@!543900561460822016> Your reasoning is because you suspect that people will want extended testing of the encoder/decoder which will delay things? <@!301186049323958275> could you put an SSZ schema for the transactions and the receipt in some appendix? <@!425279588009246720> Yeah, that is a good idea. <@!301186049323958275> I am not convinced that the benefits (although might be able to be convinced with a compelling use case) outweigh cost of including another serialization library in eth1 clients. I think it should be added to the wish list (along with no SELFDESTRUCT) for evm2.0 `uint64` or `uint32` for `cumulativeGasUsed`? 64 So we are pessimistic. 😄 I have been pursuing two EIPs to set limits to these things, but they are still somewhat in limbo. what's the hold up? Lack of time lol 🙂 Same hold up for most of the good EIPs. 😛 Is there a limit on the number of logs in a transaction? But basically it was one monster EIP which tried to do it for both the EVM and the protocol. Then we split that EIP to only be concerned with the EVM. Then finally I started to write individual EIPs for each protocol element. It was in essence agreed, but still need to execute on it. ~~Hmm, SSZ doesn't support more than 32 byte fixed width fields. So I guess logsBloom has to be in variable width section <@!364458974906548225>?~~ Nevermind, bitvector is what I need. https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1985 and https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2681 are the two merged ones. I can pursue these further if we need them due to SSZ in transactions. The suggestion on 2681 was to apply it retroactively from genesis. That would be the case for the gas limit too, etc. I'm a fan of those EIPs. Wish someone had the time to push them through. 1985 and 2681 would be awesome to get incorperated into the core protocol I can champion 2681, it seems like not much left to bring it over the finish line It seems SSZ lists are required to have a max length, which means we need to assert a max number of events in a single transaction. Most of these limits are the limits in practice because geth implements them. If gas limit is uint64, then we can safely assume that event list max is uint64.max 😬 <@!301186049323958275> there is very little overhead to setting the limit to something that we know we'll never bump up against So I guess uint64.max is the number to beat? 😛 I feel bad putting in a spec that "this array can be as big as uint64.max items long". A `LOG` is 200 gas at the minimum, right? Because that seems *obviously* wrong to me (such an array would crash any machine Ethereum runs on today). It is 200 *right now*. I don't think it necessarily has to be that high forever. Well, off you go writing a new EIP setting a hard limit for the number of logs in a tx. I suggest 65k 😬 I don't know that I could bring myself to fight for 65k. Feels too much like "256k of memory is all anyone will ever need". Hm, 65k is only 13M gas at the minimum cost. Perhaps there is potential for more logs. I would say pick a big ass number like uint32.max or uint64.max. The implications on things like SSZ proof sizes and things should be on the order of a few extra bytes. Pragmatically uint32.max sounds good. Does this size make any significant difference on the SSZ encoding? No, the encoding is the same ``` logs: List[{}, 0xffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffff] ``` the merkle proofs end up having longer paths but that stuff can all be mostly compressed away Oh, just like the zeroes out of calldata can be compressed. 😏 Max of 4 topics in a log, right? Currently. ``` Log: address: uint160 topics: List[uint256, 4] data: List[uint8, 0xffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffff] Receipt0: type: uint8 status: boolean cumulativeGasUsed: uint64 logsBloom: BitVector[2048] logs: List[Log, 0xffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffff] ``` I just did a bunch of work in Alexandria using SSZ merkle proofs for doing provable multipart transmission of data from multiple peers (basically special purpose bitttorrent). The merkle trees are dense (all the data on the left, all padding on the right, no "sparse" sections with a mixture of data/empty/data/empty. The proofs compress quite nicely. You mean just using something off the shelf like gzip? <@!301186049323958275> would it make sense having status as a number to be forward compatible? Up to `uint8` is "free". Beyond that and we are paying for extra space. > You mean just using something off the shelf like gzip? no, this: `https://notes.ethereum.org/oUJE4ZX2Q6eMOgEMiQPkpQ?view#Path-Serial

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: The underlying cryptograph spits out numbers, it seems silly to cast them to bytes since you likely just have to turn it back into a number later to use it.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: secp256k1 spits out a number (private key), which you can use to get another number (public key), which you can hash to get another number, which you can mask to get another number (address).
